4690:
A docket is an official list or schedule of things that need to be dealt with. Think of it as a formal "to-do list" — but one that belongs to an institution, not a person. It keeps track of matters that are pending, in progress, or recorded for official purposes.

This word is used in a few different but related contexts, and understanding each one will give you a complete picture.

1. A Court's Schedule of Cases (most common modern use)

In a legal setting, a docket is the official list of all cases that a court has to handle. Every lawsuit, criminal case, or legal dispute gets added to the court's docket. It tells the court: which cases exist, when they will be heard, and what stage each case is at.

Think of it like a court's appointment book — except instead of doctor visits, it's filled with legal cases.

When lawyers say a case is "on the docket," they mean it is officially scheduled and registered with the court, waiting for its turn to be heard.

When there are too many cases waiting, lawyers say the court has a "crowded docket" or "backlogged docket" — meaning the court is overwhelmed with work.

2. A Record of What Happened in a Court Case

A docket is also the official written record of everything that has happened in a specific legal case — every filing, every court order, every hearing date, every document submitted. It's essentially a case history log.

If you've ever looked up a court case online, you've seen this kind of docket. It looks like a timeline, listing entries like:

  • "Complaint filed — January 3"
  • "Defendant's response submitted — January 20"
  • "Hearing scheduled — February 10"

Each individual entry on this log is called a docket entry. The number assigned to each entry is called a docket number, which is used to identify and track that specific case across the entire court system.

3. A List of Items for Any Official Meeting or Agenda

Outside of courts, docket can also refer to a list of topics, issues, or tasks lined up for discussion or action at any official setting — a government committee, a legislative body, a formal meeting, etc.

Example: "Three major policy changes are on the docket for this week's council meeting."

Here, it simply means: these are the things officially lined up to be addressed. It's a slightly more formal way of saying "agenda."

4. A Label or Tag Attached to Goods (older and British usage)

In an older and largely British commercial sense, a docket was a physical tag, ticket, or label attached to a package, parcel, or shipment. It contained key details about the contents — what's inside, where it's going, who it's for, or what duties have been paid on it.

Think of it like the label stuck to a box at a shipping warehouse, carrying all the important information about that package.

This meaning is mostly found in historical texts, legal documents from the UK, or customs and trade contexts. In everyday modern speech, especially in American English, this sense is rare.
The Thread That Connects All the Meanings

Notice what all these meanings share: a docket is always about organizing, recording, and tracking — whether it's court cases, legal proceedings, agenda items, or packages. It's never informal or casual. A docket always implies something official, structured, and systematic.

ContextWhat "docket" means
A court (general)The full list/schedule of all cases before that court
A specific caseThe official log of everything that happened in that case
Formal meetingsThe list of items/topics lined up to be addressed
Shipping/trade (older, British)A label/tag on goods with key details

• "The judge reviewed the docket and scheduled the trial for March."

(= the court's list of cases)

  • "You can look up the docket for that lawsuit online — it shows every filing since day one."

(= the case record/log)

  • "Immigration reform is on the docket for next month's Senate session."

(= the agenda)

  • "A docket was tied to each crate, listing its contents and destination."

(= a label/tag — older usage)

The word docket is most alive today in legal and legislative settings, and whenever you hear it, the safest instinct is to think: an official, organized list of things to be handled or a record of things already handled.
4691: A doctorate is the highest level of academic degree that a university can award to a person. Think of it as the final, most advanced certificate of learning and expertise in a particular field of study. There is no academic degree above it.
The Big Picture: What It Actually Means

In most countries, education is organized in steps or levels. First, you complete school, then you go to university and earn a bachelor's degree (the basic university degree, usually 3–4 years). After that, you can pursue a master's degree (an advanced degree, usually 1–2 more years). The doctorate sits at the very top of this ladder, above both of these.

When someone holds a doctorate, it means they have not just learned a subject deeply — they have actually added new knowledge to that subject. This is the key idea that separates a doctorate from every other degree. It isn't just about studying harder or longer; it's about original contribution. The person has discovered, proven, or created something that did not exist in human knowledge before.

Earning a doctorate typically takes anywhere from 3 to 7 years of intensive work after completing a master's degree (though in some programs, you can enter directly after a bachelor's).

During this time, the student — called a doctoral student or doctoral candidate — works under the guidance of an experienced professor (called a supervisor or advisor). Their main task is to carry out original research: this means investigating a specific problem, question, or topic in great depth, often through experiments, data analysis, fieldwork, or deep theoretical study.

At the end of this long process, the student writes a very long, detailed document called a dissertation (also called a thesis in many countries). This document presents their research, their findings, and their contribution to human knowledge. It can be hundreds of pages long.

The student then defends this dissertation in front of a panel of experts — senior professors or scholars — who question them rigorously to ensure the work is genuine, original, and meets the highest academic standards. This defense is sometimes called a viva voce or simply a viva. If the panel is satisfied, the student is awarded the doctorate.

One of the most visible consequences of earning a doctorate is that the person is entitled to use the title "Dr." before their name. This is the same title used by medical doctors, and this sometimes causes confusion — but the two are distinct things (more on this below). The title signals to the world that this person is a recognized expert who has made an original contribution to their field.

The word "doctorate" is an umbrella term. There are several different kinds of doctorates, each identified by a different set of letters. Here are the most common:

Ph.D. (Doctor of Philosophy)
This is the most common and most widely recognized doctorate in the world. Despite its name, it has nothing to do with the subject of philosophy specifically. It is awarded across almost every field — sciences, humanities, engineering, social sciences, arts, and more. The name is historical, rooted in the idea that all scholarly pursuit was once considered "philosophy" (love of wisdom). When people say "I have a doctorate," they usually mean a Ph.D.

M.D. (Doctor of Medicine)
This is the doctorate awarded to medical doctors — the physicians who treat patients. In most countries, to practice as a doctor in a hospital or clinic, you need an M.D. While it is technically a doctoral-level qualification, it is a professional doctorate focused on clinical training rather than original research in the same way as a Ph.D. (though many M.D. holders also do research.)

J.D. (Juris Doctor)
This is the doctoral degree awarded to lawyers in the United States and some other countries. It qualifies a person to practice law.

Ed.D. (Doctor of Education)
This is awarded to people who specialize in education systems, educational leadership, or teaching at the highest academic level.

D.B.A. (Doctor of Business Administration)
This is the doctoral degree in business and management.

There are many others — D.Phil., D.Sc., Psy.D., D.D.S., and more — but they all share the same fundamental characteristic: they represent the highest level of qualification in their respective fields.

It helps to understand that doctorates come in two broad categories:

A research doctorate (like a Ph.D.) is focused on producing new knowledge. The entire degree is built around conducting original research and contributing something new to the world's understanding of a subject.

A professional doctorate (like an M.D. or J.D.) is focused on qualifying someone to practice a profession at the highest level. While these degrees are rigorous and demanding, their primary purpose is professional preparation rather than original research contribution.

Both are genuinely called doctorates. Both earn the holder the right to use the title "Dr." Both are the highest qualification in their respective fields. The distinction is mainly in their purpose and structure.

In everyday speech, "doctorate" is used in a few consistent ways:

  • "She holds a doctorate in physics." — meaning she has earned the degree.
  • "He is pursuing a doctorate." — meaning he is currently working toward the degree.
  • "The doctorate took her five years to complete." — referring to the degree as a process or achievement.
  • "A doctorate is required for this position." — meaning the employer demands this level of qualification.

The related adjective is doctoral: "doctoral research," "doctoral thesis," "doctoral student." These simply mean "related to or involving a doctorate."

Beyond the personal achievement, a doctorate carries real-world weight in several ways:

In academia: A doctorate is essentially a mandatory credential to become a professor or researcher at a university. Without it, you generally cannot hold a permanent academic position or lead independent research.

In research institutions: Government research bodies, think tanks, pharmaceutical companies, and scientific institutions typically require or strongly prefer doctoral-level qualifications for senior research roles.

In some professions: In medicine and law (in countries where the M.D. and J.D. are standard), it is a professional license, not optional.

In society: A doctorate signals deep expertise. When someone with a doctorate speaks about their field, the credential tells you they have not merely read about the subject — they have spent years at the frontier of it.
These two phrases mean exactly the same thing. "A doctorate" and "a doctoral degree" are interchangeable. People use both freely.
The Full Picture in One Sentence

A doctorate is the highest academic degree awarded by a university, earned after years of original research and the successful defense of a dissertation, and it marks the holder as someone who has genuinely expanded the boundaries of human knowledge in their chosen field.
4692:
When we call someone or something doctrinaire, we mean they are rigidly, inflexibly devoted to a theory or set of beliefs — and they apply that theory mechanically, no matter what the real world is actually telling them.

A doctrine is a set of principles or beliefs that forms a system of thought — a political ideology, an economic theory, a religious teaching, a philosophical framework, and so on. A doctrinaire person treats their doctrine as sacred and untouchable. They take it as a perfect, complete instruction manual for reality, and they refuse to bend it even slightly, even when the facts on the ground scream for a different approach.
The Key Thing That Makes Something "Doctrinaire"

The heart of this word is a specific kind of intellectual stubbornness: the theory always wins. Evidence, exceptions, practical consequences, common sense — none of these things are allowed to challenge or soften the doctrine. The doctrinaire person doesn't ask "does my theory work here?" They ask "how do I apply my theory here?" — and those are very different questions.

This is what separates doctrinaire thinking from simply being principled or consistent. A principled person holds firm to their values but stays open to adjusting their approach when reality pushes back. A doctrinaire person does not adjust. The doctrine is always right, and if reality disagrees with the doctrine, then reality is the problem.
The Tone: It's Almost Always Critical

This is an important thing to know: doctrinaire is nearly always used as a criticism. When you call someone doctrinaire, you are not complimenting their dedication or consistency. You are accusing them of being impractical, closed-minded, and out of touch — someone who is so in love with the tidiness of their theory that they've lost the ability to think freshly about the messy, complicated world in front of them.

It carries a faint air of intellectual arrogance too — the implication that the doctrinaire person believes their system has already solved everything, and that anyone who questions it simply doesn't understand it well enough.

Example 1 — Economics:
A finance minister is dealing with a severe economic recession. Citizens are losing jobs, poverty is rising, and experts are calling for government spending to stimulate the economy. But the minister refuses. He has spent his whole career believing that governments must never run budget deficits under any circumstances. He cuts spending instead, making things worse. A journalist writes: "His doctrinaire commitment to fiscal austerity made him blind to the humanitarian emergency unfolding before him."

He's not evil — he genuinely believes in his economic theory. But he applies it like a machine, refusing to let reality modify it even temporarily.

Example 2 — Politics:
A revolutionary leader takes power with a brilliant vision for a fair society. But instead of adapting his ideas as he learns what actually works, he insists on following his political doctrine to the letter, even as the consequences cause suffering. Critics call him "a doctrinaire ideologue more interested in theoretical purity than in the wellbeing of actual people."

Example 3 — Everyday life:
A manager believes strictly that employees should never be given flexibility in their hours — that's the rule, full stop. An employee has a genuine family emergency and asks to shift her schedule temporarily. The manager refuses, because the policy says no flexibility. A colleague remarks: "He's so doctrinaire about the rules that he can't even apply basic human judgment."

In all three cases, you can see the same pattern: a theory is being applied rigidly, at the expense of thinking clearly about the specific, real situation at hand.
The Subtle Shade of Meaning: Theory Over People

One reason this word feels particularly pointed as a criticism is that it implies the person has essentially reversed the proper relationship between ideas and reality. Ideas are supposed to be tools we use to understand and improve the real world. A doctrinaire thinker treats their doctrine as the master, and the real world as something that must conform to it. This gets things backwards — and often causes real harm to real people in the process.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Dogmatic is the closest word, and the two are often used interchangeably. But there's a subtle difference: dogmatic emphasizes asserting beliefs as absolute, unchallengeable truth — often with a sense of authority or even aggression. Doctrinaire emphasizes the application of a theoretical system in a rigid, inflexible way — it's a bit more intellectual and systematic in character. A dogmatic person says "this is the truth and I won't hear otherwise." A doctrinaire person says "my system has the answer for this, and I will apply it."

Rigid is more general — it just means inflexible. Doctrinaire specifically ties that inflexibility to a body of doctrine or theory.

Ideological is neutral — it simply means "relating to an ideology." Doctrinaire takes that same territory and adds the criticism of inflexibility and impracticality.

Fanatical suggests extreme passion and emotional intensity. Doctrinaire is cooler and more cerebral in tone — it's the inflexibility of a theorist, not the fire of a zealot.
Where You'll Typically See This Word

Doctrinaire shows up most often in political writing, journalism, economic debates, and intellectual criticism. It's a formal, somewhat sophisticated word — you're unlikely to hear it in casual conversation, but you'll encounter it in newspapers, essays, and political commentary regularly. Common pairings include things like "doctrinaire Marxist," "doctrinaire free-market ideology," "doctrinaire approach," or "doctrinaire insistence on X."

If you need to boil it down to one sentence: Doctrinaire describes a way of thinking or a person who applies a theory or doctrine with such rigid, inflexible devotion that they lose sight of practical reality — and won't let the messiness of the real world challenge or soften their system.
4693:
A doctrinaire is a person who holds a set of principles or theories so rigidly that they insist on applying them to every situation — regardless of whether doing so actually works, causes harm, or flies in the face of reality.

The key thing to understand is this: a doctrinaire cares more about the purity of their theory than about real-world results. They are not stupid or necessarily ignorant — they may even be very intelligent and well-read. But they are intellectually inflexible to a fault. When theory collides with reality, a doctrinaire sides with the theory, every single time.

Imagine someone who has read extensively about a particular economic system and has become deeply convinced it is the perfect solution to poverty. A wise person would say, "Let's try it carefully, observe the results, and adjust if things go wrong."

A doctrinaire would say, "The theory is correct. If it isn't working, it's because people aren't following it correctly. We must apply it more strictly." They double down. They refuse to modify their position based on evidence. The doctrine is sacred to them.

That's the doctrinaire.

This is not a neutral word. Calling someone a doctrinaire is a criticism. It implies:

  • Stubbornness disguised as conviction. They look principled, but they're actually just unable or unwilling to think flexibly.
  • Arrogance. There's a quiet suggestion that they trust their theory more than they trust the messy, complicated truth of real life.
  • Impracticality. Their insistence on theoretical purity makes them useless — or even dangerous — when it comes to solving real problems.

When someone is called a doctrinaire, the speaker is essentially saying: "This person is so trapped inside their own belief system that they can no longer engage honestly with the world."

The word appears most often in political, philosophical, and intellectual contexts. Some examples of how it's used:

  • A politician who refuses to compromise on any policy, insisting every law must conform perfectly to their ideology — even when the result is gridlock or suffering — might be called a doctrinaire.
  • An economist who insists a particular economic model must be applied in its "pure" form, even when it's causing mass unemployment, is a doctrinaire.
  • A religious thinker who demands that every life situation must be addressed by strict, literal application of religious law — without any room for human judgment or context — could be called a doctrinaire.
  • Even in something like education, a teacher who insists their one method is the only correct method of teaching, refusing to adapt even when students aren't learning, is behaving like a doctrinaire.
What Makes a Doctrinaire Different from Similar People

It helps to compare the doctrinaire with a few related types of people, because these words get confused:

A fanatic or zealot is driven by intense, often emotional passion. They are fervent, sometimes violent or extreme in their devotion. A doctrinaire, however, operates more calmly — with intellectual certainty rather than raw emotion. The doctrinaire's inflexibility is cooler, more cerebral.

A dogmatist asserts that certain beliefs are absolutely true and beyond question. The dogmatist is about what you must believe. The doctrinaire is a step further — about how you must act on those beliefs, insisting that the theory must be applied systematically to real situations without compromise or modification.

An idealist believes strongly in a vision of how the world could or should be. An idealist is not necessarily a doctrinaire — idealists can still adapt their approach. A doctrinaire takes idealism to its stiff, impractical extreme.

Think of it this way: a doctrinaire is someone who has turned a set of ideas into a rulebook, and then decided the rulebook must be followed perfectly — even when the rulebook is clearly failing.
The Deeper Problem with a Doctrinaire

The real danger of a doctrinaire is not just stubbornness — it's a specific kind of intellectual dishonesty. By deciding that the theory must be right, they stop honestly looking at what's actually happening around them. Evidence becomes an enemy rather than a guide.

This is why the word carries such a sharp critical sting. We generally believe that a thoughtful, honest person updates their views when reality pushes back. A doctrinaire refuses to do this. They are, in a sense, at war with reality — and they've chosen to keep losing that war rather than reconsider their position.
A One-Line Summary to Lock It In

A doctrinaire is someone who is so devoted to a theory or doctrine that they insist it must be applied rigidly in all situations, refusing to adapt even when the real world clearly demands it — making them impractical, inflexible, and dangerously disconnected from reality.
4694:
A doctrine is a set of beliefs, principles, or rules that a group officially accepts, teaches, and follows. Think of it as the "official position" of a group — whether that group is a religion, a government, a military, a political party, a legal system, or a school of thought.

A doctrine is not just any random opinion or idea. It has three defining qualities that together make it a doctrine. First, it is formal and official — it comes from a recognized authority, not from a private individual's thoughts. Second, it is taught — it is actively passed down to others who belong to that group or institution. Third, it is collectively held — a defined group of people stand behind it together, not just one person alone.

This is why we say a church has a "doctrine" but an individual person usually just has "beliefs" or "opinions." The moment a belief becomes the official, taught position of a recognized group, it earns the name doctrine.
Doctrine in different areas of life

The word "doctrine" is used in several important areas, and understanding each one will give you a complete picture.

In religion, doctrine refers to the formal teachings of a faith. The Christian "doctrine of the Trinity," for example, holds that God exists as three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is not a personal opinion of individual Christians; it is the officially established and actively taught position of the church. When someone says a person is "doctrinally sound," they mean that person's beliefs match what their church officially teaches.

In law, doctrine refers to an established legal principle that courts rely on when making decisions. Legal doctrines develop over time through court rulings and eventually become binding rules in the justice system. The "doctrine of precedent," for instance, requires courts to follow earlier decisions when handling similar cases. The "fair use doctrine" in copyright law sets out the specific conditions under which someone may use copyrighted material without needing permission.

In politics and government, leaders use the word doctrine to describe the official principles guiding their foreign or domestic policy. The "Monroe Doctrine" (1823) was a declaration of U.S. foreign policy stating that the Americas were closed to further European colonization. When a government announces a doctrine, it is publicly committing to a set of principles that will shape its decisions going forward.

In the military, doctrine refers to the fundamental, standardized principles that guide how armed forces operate, fight, and are organized. Military doctrine is typically written and official so that all soldiers and commanders are working from the same foundation. It answers the question: "How do we, as a military force, believe warfare should be conducted?"

In philosophy and academia, a doctrine is a formal position or set of positions held by a philosopher or a school of thought. The "doctrine of empiricism," for example, holds that all human knowledge originates from sensory experience.
How doctrine differs from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so read this section carefully.

A belief is broader and more personal. It is simply something an individual thinks is true. A doctrine is a formally established belief held and actively taught by a group. Every doctrine begins as a belief, but not every belief becomes a doctrine.

A theory is an explanation of how something works, usually in science. A scientific theory is meant to be tested, challenged, and potentially revised as new evidence emerges. A doctrine, by contrast, carries authority — within the group that holds it, it is generally not up for open debate in the same way a scientific theory is.

A principle is a single fundamental truth or rule — honesty, fairness, or conservation of energy, for example. A doctrine is broader; it is a comprehensive, officially taught system that may contain many principles within it.

An ideology is a full system of ideas and values that shapes how a group sees the entire political or social world — liberalism, conservatism, and Marxism are ideologies. An ideology is larger in scope than a doctrine. A doctrine might be one specific part of a broader ideology.

A rule is a specific instruction about what to do or not do. A doctrine is the deeper belief or reasoning that sits behind rules and gives them their justification.

Dogma is the word most often confused with doctrine, and they are closely related. Dogma refers to beliefs that must be accepted as absolutely and unquestionably true, especially in a religious context. All dogma is doctrine, but not all doctrine is dogma. Dogma carries a stronger, more rigid sense — "you must believe this without question." Doctrine is the broader, slightly softer term that can sometimes allow for scholarly interpretation and internal discussion within the group, even while remaining the official position.

In most professional and academic contexts, "doctrine" is a perfectly neutral word — a military officer, a theologian, and a lawyer all use it without any emotional charge. However, in everyday informal conversation, the word can sometimes carry a slightly rigid or inflexible feeling. When someone says, "She follows that doctrine blindly," they are suggesting that the person accepts the belief without questioning it. This subtle tone of inflexibility appears mostly in informal or critical usage, not in formal writing, so be aware of the context when you encounter it.

The plural is doctrines. You use it when referring to multiple separate sets of beliefs or principles. For example: "The two churches share certain doctrines but disagree sharply on others." You can also use it to refer to the collection of teachings within a single system: "The doctrines of Buddhism are taught in monasteries across Asia."

"The military published its updated combat doctrine last year."

"The legal doctrine of innocent until proven guilty is central to any fair justice system."

"The party's economic doctrine favors low taxes and limited government intervention."

"She spent years studying the doctrines of early Christianity."

"The president's foreign policy doctrine was controversial from the moment it was announced."

"These two philosophies rest on entirely different doctrines about the nature of reality."
The single most important thing to remember

If you ever forget every detail above, remember this: a doctrine is the official, taught belief of a group. It is not personal, not informal, and not up for casual renegotiation within the group that holds it. It is what a recognized authority has formally established and what members of that group are expected to accept and carry forward. That is the heart of the word.
4695: A document is a piece of recorded information. The key word here is recorded — it means the information has been fixed in some form so that it can be preserved, referred to, shared, or used later. A thought in your head is not a document. The moment you write it down on paper, type it into a file, or capture it in any stable form, it starts to become one.

Think of a document as a container that holds information in a durable way. That information might be facts, instructions, agreements, proof of something, or simply a message. What makes it a document rather than just "writing" is that it has some level of permanence and purpose — it exists so that someone can read it, use it, or refer back to it.

A document is always about something. It represents or records something that happened, something that was agreed upon, something that is true, or something that needs to be communicated.

Documents can exist in two broad forms:

A physical document is one you can hold in your hand — a piece of paper, a card, a printed sheet. A birth certificate, a letter, a signed contract, a printed invoice — these are all physical documents.

A digital document is stored electronically — on a computer, a phone, a server. A PDF file, a Word file, a text file, a spreadsheet, an email — these are digital documents. Even a webpage can be considered a document in the broader sense. The word "document" now comfortably covers both forms, and in modern usage, digital documents are just as valid and common as paper ones.

Documents exist on a wide spectrum from very formal to very informal.

Formal or official documents are those that carry legal, governmental, or institutional weight. They often follow a specific format, are issued by an authority, and serve as binding proof of something. Examples:

  • A passport — official proof of your identity and nationality, issued by a government
  • A contract — a written agreement between two or more parties that is legally binding
  • A degree certificate — proof that you completed an academic programme
  • A property deed — legal record of who owns a piece of land or building
  • A will — a legal document stating how a person's belongings should be distributed after death
  • A court order — an official instruction from a court

These documents matter enormously because they can be used as evidence, they have authority, and they are often protected by law. Losing or forging them has serious consequences.

Informal documents are everyday written records that don't carry legal weight but are still useful for communication, reference, or record-keeping. Examples: a memo between colleagues, a shopping list (loosely), a personal diary entry, an internal report, a draft proposal, or meeting notes. These are documents too, just without the weight of official status.

Understanding a document fully means understanding what job it does. Documents generally serve one or more of these roles:

1. Recording information
A document captures something so it isn't lost. Minutes of a meeting, a scientific report, a historical account — these exist so that information can survive beyond the moment it was created and be available to others, including people in the future.

2. Proving something
Many documents exist as evidence. A receipt proves you paid for something. A birth certificate proves you were born on a certain date. An employment contract proves you were hired under specific terms. This evidentiary function is one of the most important reasons documents exist — they are trusted because they are concrete and verifiable.

3. Communicating information
A document can be a vehicle for sharing information from one person or organisation to another. A report, a letter, a manual, a policy — these communicate something from a writer to a reader, sometimes immediately, sometimes across time.

4. Authorising or instructing
Some documents give permission or issue instructions. A doctor's prescription authorises a pharmacist to dispense medicine. A warrant authorises the police to search a location. A user manual instructs someone on how to use a product.

5. Creating a formal record
Organisations, governments, and institutions constantly generate documents to create an official record of decisions, events, and transactions. Tax filings, audit reports, board meeting minutes — these exist so there is a trail of what happened and what was decided.

The word "document" is used fairly broadly, but there are degrees. In everyday speech, people tend to use it for:

  • Formal written records (government papers, legal papers)
  • Any file you work with on a computer (especially in apps like Microsoft Word or Google Docs, where a "document" is simply a text file you create)
  • Any written piece that is meant to be preserved, shared, or referred to

You would not normally call a sticky note with a phone number a "document," but you might call a formal letter one. The more structured, purposeful, and lasting something is, the more naturally the word "document" applies. However, in technical or digital contexts, the word is used quite loosely — even a simple text file can be called a document.
A Document vs. a Book vs. a Record

These words are related but distinct, and it helps to see the difference:

  • A book is usually a longer, structured work meant for reading as a whole — a novel, a textbook. Not all books are documents, though some (like historical texts, legal codes, or reference books) can be.
  • A record often refers to a piece of stored data, especially in databases or administrative systems. Every document is a kind of record, but not every record is a document — a row in a spreadsheet database is a record, not usually a document.
  • A document sits in the middle: it is a human-readable piece of written or recorded information that has a defined purpose and some degree of permanence.

A document is a recorded, durable piece of information — written, printed, or stored electronically — that serves a purpose: to preserve facts, communicate something, prove a claim, or establish an official record. Documents can be as formal as a legal contract or as simple as a memo. They can exist on paper or as a digital file. What ties all of them together is that they capture information in a fixed form so it can be used, referenced, shared, or verified — now or in the future. This is why documents are fundamental to law, government, business, science, education, and everyday life.
4696:
Documentary as an adjective means: based on, consisting of, or relating to documents and factual records.

Think of it this way — a document is any recorded piece of evidence about reality: a written letter, a photograph, a video clip, an official paper, a signed contract. The adjective documentary describes anything that is built from or grounded in such real records.
What It Really Means in Practice

When you call something "documentary," you are making a strong claim: this is rooted in reality, not imagination. You are saying the thing being described draws from actual facts, real events, or genuine evidence — rather than being invented or fictional.

It answers the question: "Is this made up, or is it real?" — and documentary firmly answers: "It is real. Here is the evidence."
The Two Main Areas Where You'll Encounter It

1. Documentary Evidence / Proof

This is the most literal use. In law, history, journalism, and research, "documentary evidence" means evidence that exists in the form of documents — written records, photographs, audio recordings, official certificates, contracts, diaries, and so on.

For example:

  • A court might demand documentary proof of your identity — meaning actual papers, not just your word.
  • A historian might rely on documentary sources — meaning original letters, government records, or archived newspapers — rather than just oral stories passed down through generations.

Here, documentary is the opposite of oral, hearsay, or anecdotal. It implies something you can show, read, and verify.

2. Documentary Films, Photography, and Storytelling

When applied to art forms — film, photography, television, writing — documentary means the work is a faithful record of real life, not a fictional story.

A documentary film captures real people, real events, real places. It uses real footage, real interviews, real evidence. Nothing is scripted or performed. The filmmaker is saying: "I recorded reality."

Similarly, documentary photography means photos taken to truthfully record life as it actually is — a photograph of a war, a famine, daily life in a community — not a staged or edited fantasy image.

The key idea here: a documentary work bears witness. It says, "This actually happened. I have the record."
The Deeper Meaning: Why "Documentary" Carries Weight

The word carries an implied promise of truthfulness. When something is described as documentary, there is an understood commitment that it:

  • Comes from real sources, not from someone's imagination
  • Can, at least in principle, be verified by looking at the underlying records
  • Aims to accurately represent what actually happened or existed

This is why the word matters. In a world where things can be easily fabricated or distorted, calling something documentary is a way of saying: "I can show you my sources. The evidence exists. This is not invented."

Documentary ≠ completely unbiased. Even a documentary film or a documentary account is shaped by the choices of whoever made it — which records to include, which to leave out, how to frame events. The word tells you the material is real; it does not guarantee the interpretation is perfectly neutral. This is an important distinction.

Degree matters. Sometimes "documentary" is used to describe an approach or style, not just a strict category. A book can be written "in a documentary style" — meaning it heavily relies on real records, quotes from real people, and factual accounts, even if it is not a pure document itself.

"Documentary" vs. "documented." These are easy to confuse. Documented means "having been recorded or proved by documents" (a well-documented case). Documentary means "of the nature of, or consisting of, documents or factual records" (documentary evidence). Documented describes something that has been supported by records. Documentary describes something that is itself a record or is built from records.

Whenever you see the adjective documentary, ask yourself: "Does this rely on actual, real records of the world?" If yes — that's documentary. It means: real, record-based, grounded in actual evidence.

SentenceWhat "documentary" means here
"The lawyer presented documentary evidence."Evidence in the form of actual documents (letters, contracts, photos)
"She directed a documentary film about climate scientists."A film recording real people and real events — not fiction
"The archive holds a documentary record of the city's history."A record built from real primary sources
"He has documentary proof of the payment."Physical/written proof you can actually see and read

Documentary, as an adjective, describes anything that is built from real records and factual evidence — things you can actually see, read, or verify — rather than being invented, imagined, or passed on merely by word of mouth.
4697:
A documentary is a film, video, or television program that is about real things — real events, real people, real places, or real issues. Nothing in it is invented for the purpose of entertainment. It is the opposite of fiction.

When you watch a fictional movie, actors play characters that don't exist, in situations that were written by a screenwriter. A documentary throws all of that out. Instead, it films the actual world — what really happened, who was really there, and what things really look like.
What makes a documentary different from other things

From a fictional film: A fictional film tells a made-up story. A documentary records or examines a real one.

From a news report: A news report is usually very short — a few minutes — and sticks to the basic facts of a recent event. A documentary goes much deeper. It explores a topic from multiple angles, provides background and history, includes interviews with several people, and often takes 45 minutes to several hours. It tries to give you a full, rich understanding of something.

From a textbook or article: A documentary uses the visual medium. Instead of just reading about something, you see it. You watch actual footage, hear real voices, and observe real places. This makes the learning experience far more immersive and emotional.
What you typically find inside a documentary

Most documentaries are built from a combination of these elements:

Real footage — Video recorded of actual events, places, or people as they happen or exist. This is the backbone of any documentary.

Interviews — Real people speak on camera about the topic. These might be experts (scientists, historians, doctors), eyewitnesses, survivors, participants, or ordinary people affected by the subject.

Narration — A voice (often unseen) guides you through the topic, providing context, explanation, and transitions between scenes. Sometimes the narrator is the filmmaker themselves.

Archival material — Old photographs, historical footage, newspaper clippings, maps, letters, and other documents from the past, used to show you things that couldn't be filmed today.

Re-enactments — Occasionally, when an important event was never filmed, actors may briefly recreate it. However, good documentaries clearly signal when this is happening, so the viewer is never misled into thinking they're watching real footage.
The purpose of a documentary

A documentary is made to do one or more of these things:

  • Inform and educate — to teach you something about the world you didn't know before.
  • Preserve history — to create a record of events, people, or cultures so they are not forgotten.
  • Raise awareness — to bring attention to a problem, injustice, or situation that many people are unaware of.
  • Provoke thought — to ask difficult questions and encourage the viewer to think critically about an issue.
  • Persuade — some documentaries are made with a clear agenda: the filmmaker wants you to agree with their position. These are sometimes called advocacy documentaries. (More on this below.)
Types of documentaries

Over the decades, filmmakers have developed different styles and approaches. Here are the main ones:

Expository documentary — This is the most classic and familiar type. A narrator speaks over visuals, guiding the audience through the subject in an organized, informative way. Nature documentaries narrated by David Attenborough — like Planet Earth — are the best-known example of this style. It feels like a knowledgeable guide explaining something to you.

Observational documentary (also called "fly-on-the-wall") — The filmmaker films without narrating or interfering. The camera simply watches as events unfold naturally. The idea is to show life as it really is, without the filmmaker's voice shaping your understanding. The audience draws their own conclusions. This style aims for a feeling of pure observation.

Participatory documentary — Here, the filmmaker becomes part of the story. They appear on screen, ask questions directly to people, and sometimes insert themselves into the situations they're filming. American filmmaker Michael Moore is well known for this style — he frequently appears on camera, confronting people and companies about issues like gun violence or corporate greed.

Poetic documentary — This type is less focused on facts and more focused on emotion, mood, and visual beauty. It might not have a clear narrative or even much dialogue — it creates an experience more than it delivers information.

Reflexive documentary — This style is self-aware and questions the documentary form itself. It draws attention to the fact that a filmmaker is making choices about what to show and how. It reminds the viewer that even documentaries are constructed, not just neutral windows into reality.
An important truth: documentaries are not perfectly objective

This is one of the most important things to understand about documentaries. Many people assume that because a documentary is about real things, it must be presenting the full, unbiased truth. But this is not always the case.

Every documentary is shaped by the choices of its maker:

  • What topic did they choose to cover?
  • Which people did they choose to interview?
  • What footage did they include, and what did they leave out?
  • What music is playing in the background, and how does it make you feel?
  • In what order is the information presented?

All of these choices influence how you feel about the subject. A skilled documentarian can use real footage and real facts to make you feel a certain way — without lying to you, but by emphasizing certain things and downplaying others.

This is why it's important to think critically when watching a documentary, especially one that deals with a controversial topic. Ask yourself: Whose voice is missing here? What's the other side of this story?
Documentary film vs. documentary series

A documentary can take two forms:

A documentary film is a standalone piece, typically ranging from about 45 minutes to over two hours, viewed in one sitting (in a cinema or on a screen at home).

A documentary series is a multi-episode work, where each episode covers a different aspect of the topic or a different story. You watch it over several sessions. Many of the most popular documentaries today, especially on streaming platforms like Netflix, are series.
Documentary vs. docudrama — a common confusion

A docudrama is different from a documentary. A docudrama uses professional actors to dramatize and recreate real historical events. It tells a real story, but through performance, scripted dialogue, and cinematic techniques. The result looks more like a regular film than a documentary.

A documentary, by contrast, relies on actual footage and real people — not actors playing those people.
Common subjects that documentaries cover

Documentaries can be made about virtually anything, but the most common subjects include:

  • Nature and wildlife — animals, ecosystems, oceans, and the natural world
  • History — wars, civilizations, significant events, historical figures
  • Social issues — poverty, inequality, discrimination, human rights
  • True crime — investigations into real crimes, court cases, and injustices
  • Politics and power — governments, elections, corruption, movements
  • Science and technology — space exploration, medicine, artificial intelligence
  • Environment — climate change, deforestation, pollution
  • Biography — the life of a notable or fascinating individual
  • Sports — athletes, teams, or landmark events in sports history
  • Culture and art — music, film, religion, food, fashion
Well-known examples

To make this concrete, here are some famous documentaries and what they're about:

  • Planet Earth (BBC, 2006) — A landmark nature series narrated by David Attenborough, showing the beauty and diversity of life on Earth across different environments. Expository style at its finest.
  • Making a Murderer (Netflix, 2015) — A true crime series that follows the case of Steven Avery, a Wisconsin man convicted of murder, raising serious questions about the justice system.
  • 13th (Netflix, 2016) — An examination of racial inequality in the United States, specifically looking at the prison system and how it connects to the history of slavery.
  • Free Solo (2018) — A film following rock climber Alex Honnold as he attempts to climb a nearly vertical 900-metre rock face in Yosemite, California, with no ropes.
  • Blackfish (2013) — A documentary about killer whales (orcas) kept in captivity at SeaWorld, exposing the conditions of their captivity and incidents of violence. It was so impactful it led to major policy changes.
  • Super Size Me (2004) — Filmmaker Morgan Spurlock eats only McDonald's food for 30 days and documents what happens to his body and health. A clear example of a participatory, advocacy-style documentary.
Where documentaries are found

You can watch documentaries in:

  • Cinemas — Many documentaries are released in theatres, especially award-nominated ones.
  • Streaming platforms — Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV+, Disney+, and others produce and host large libraries of documentaries and documentary series.
  • Television channels — BBC, National Geographic, Discovery Channel, PBS (in the US), and similar channels have been a home for documentaries for decades.
  • Film festivals — Major festivals like Sundance, Tribeca, and IDFA (International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam) are dedicated to showcasing documentary films.
In summary

A documentary is a non-fiction audiovisual work that explores the real world — real events, real people, real places, and real issues — using actual footage, interviews, narration, and archival material. Its purpose is to inform, educate, preserve, raise awareness, or persuade. It differs from fiction in that nothing is invented, and from news in that it goes much deeper. It comes in many styles — from calm, narrated nature films to confrontational, participatory social investigations — and covers almost any subject you can imagine. While it is grounded in reality, it is always shaped by the choices of the person who made it, so it should be watched with a thoughtful and critical eye.
4698: Documentation is any written, recorded, or organized material that captures information — so that the information can be understood, used, referred back to, or proven later. Think of it as "putting things down in a form that lasts and communicates."

When something important happens, gets created, or needs to be explained, you can't just keep it only in someone's head. What if that person leaves? What if you forget? What if someone else needs to understand it? Documentation solves this. It is the act — and the result — of recording information in a clear, organized, and accessible way.

So "documentation" refers to:

  • The process of creating such records
  • The collection of records themselves

Both meanings are common, and context makes clear which one is meant.

Almost anything worth remembering or communicating:

  • A process or procedure — the steps to do something (e.g., how to operate a machine, how to file a tax return)
  • A decision — what was decided, by whom, and why
  • An agreement — what two or more parties promised each other (contracts, policies)
  • A product or system — how something works, how to use it, what its parts are
  • An event — what happened, when, and who was involved
  • An identity or status — proof of who you are or what qualifications you hold (e.g., a passport, a certificate, a medical record)

Documentation does not mean only paper. It includes:

  • Manuals and guides
  • Reports and summaries
  • Official certificates and licenses
  • Emails and letters (when kept as records)
  • Photographs, videos, audio recordings
  • Logs and registers (like a hospital patient's file)
  • Software comments and technical write-ups
  • Legal papers and contracts

What all of these share is intent: they are created deliberately to preserve and communicate information.

Documentation serves several important purposes:

  1. Memory — Humans forget. Organizations grow. Documentation ensures important information survives beyond individual memory.
  2. Clarity — When instructions or decisions are written down carefully, there is less room for misunderstanding or miscommunication.
  3. Proof — Documentation can serve as evidence. Your birth certificate documents your birth. A signed receipt documents a transaction. In disputes, documentation is often the deciding factor.
  4. Consistency — When a process is documented, every person who follows it can do so the same way. This is critical in medicine, law, engineering, and many other fields.
  5. Learning and onboarding — When someone new joins a team or studies a subject, documentation helps them get up to speed without needing someone to explain everything from scratch.
  6. Accountability — Records of who did what, when, and why create accountability, which is important in workplaces, governments, and legal systems.

The word is used across many fields, and while the core meaning stays the same, the flavor changes slightly:

  • In software and technology, documentation refers to written explanations of how a program or system works — for users ("user documentation") or for developers ("technical documentation"). Good software documentation makes the difference between a tool people can use and one that frustrates them.
  • In medicine, documentation means patient records — symptoms, diagnoses, treatments, test results. Accurate medical documentation is a legal and ethical obligation.
  • In law and business, documentation refers to the formal papers and records that support a claim, a transaction, a contract, or a project. "Do you have documentation for that?" means "Can you prove it with written records?"
  • In immigration, documentation refers to official papers that prove your identity, nationality, or legal status (passport, visa, work permit).
  • In research and academia, documentation means citing your sources and keeping records of your data and methods — so others can verify or build upon your work.

A document is a single item — one paper, one file, one record.

Documentation (usually uncountable, or treated as a collective noun) refers to the whole body of such material. For example, "the documentation for this software" means all the manuals, guides, and reference materials together — not just one page.

However, "documentations" (plural) is occasionally used when referring to several distinct sets of records or bodies of documentation — though this is less common.
A simple way to remember it

If you ever wonder what documentation means, ask yourself: "Has this been written down properly so someone else can understand, use, verify, or learn from it?" If the answer is yes, what you're holding — or what was created — is documentation.
4699: Doddering is an adjective that describes a person — almost always an elderly one — who has become noticeably weak, shaky, and mentally slow due to old age. It paints a picture of someone whose body and mind are both clearly in decline. Think of a very old man shuffling across the room with trembling hands, forgetting what he just said, and struggling to follow a basic conversation. That is a doddering person.

When you call someone doddering, you are pointing to a combination of physical and mental traits — not just one or the other.

Physically, a doddering person:

  • Moves very slowly and unsteadily, often with a shuffling walk
  • Has shaky, trembling hands or limbs
  • Appears frail and fragile, like they could lose their balance easily
  • Lacks the strength and coordination they once had

Mentally, a doddering person:

  • Is forgetful and easily confused
  • Struggles to think clearly or keep up with what is happening around them
  • May repeat themselves without realizing it
  • Seems "out of it" — not fully present or sharp

The key point is that both things happen together. Doddering is not just being physically old and slow, and it is not just being a little forgetful. It is when both the body and the mind seem to be failing together, making the person appear helpless and incompetent in a very visible way.

This is where many learners miss something important. "Doddering" is not a neutral word. It carries a tone of mild contempt or dismissiveness. When someone describes a person as doddering, they are not being kind or sympathetic — they are suggesting that this person is no longer capable, no longer useful, and perhaps even a bit pitiable or laughable.

It is the kind of word you might use when you are frustrated with an old person's incompetence, or when you want to make someone seem past their prime and out of touch. For example, if someone says "that doddering old fool," they are not just describing old age — they are being dismissive and a little unkind.

This is worth remembering: the word has a slight edge to it. It subtly implies that the person is not just old, but uselessly old.

Doddering is almost exclusively used for elderly people. You would not call a young or middle-aged person doddering unless you were being very sarcastic or making a strong exaggerated point. The word is bound to old age — it describes what happens when age takes away a person's physical steadiness and mental sharpness at the same time.

These will help you see the word in action across different contexts:

  • The doddering old professor could barely remember his students' names anymore.
  • Critics dismissed the politician as a doddering fool who had no business running the country.
  • She watched her once-sharp grandfather become doddering and confused over the years.
  • The new CEO was brought in to replace the doddering leadership that had been running the company into the ground.
  • He moved across the stage in a doddering manner, pausing every few steps to steady himself.

Notice that in each sentence, the word signals both physical frailty and mental decline — and carries a tone that is not exactly compassionate.

Think of a scale from "slightly old" to "completely falling apart." Doddering sits toward the stronger end. It is not used for someone who is just a little slow or just slightly forgetful. It is used when the decline is noticeable and significant enough to affect how the person functions — when it is obvious to everyone watching that this person is not the way they used to be.

It is easy to confuse "doddering" with simply meaning "old." But old age alone does not make someone doddering. A sharp, strong, independent 85-year-old is not doddering. The word only applies when age has brought with it a clear loss of physical steadiness and mental sharpness, to the point where the person seems feeble and out of touch with what is going on around them. That combination — frail body, clouded mind, visible incompetence — is what "doddering" truly captures.
